symptoms: Olive-green to dark brown or black velvety spots on leaves.
Lesions may cause leaf distortion, curling, and premature defoliation.
Scabby, cracked lesions on developing fruit surfaces.
causes: Associated with the ascomycete fungus Venturia inaequalis.
Overwinters in fallen infected leaves on the orchard floor.
environment: Cool, wet spring weather (55°F to 75°F / 13°C to 24°C)
Extended periods of leaf wetness (>6 hours)
High relative humidity
spread: Primary ascospores released from overwintered leaves via rain splash and wind.
Secondary conidia spread during summer rain events.
immediate_actions: Inspect orchard canopy for new velvety foliar lesions.
Remove or shred fallen leaves to accelerate decomposition.
Prune dense canopy branches to improve air circulation and sunlight penetration.
prevention: Plant scab-resistant cultivars (e.g., Liberty, Enterprise, GoldRush).
Apply protective fungicides prior to projected spring wetting events according to Mills infection periods.
Practice orchard floor sanitation through autumn flail mowing or urea application to fallen leaves.
apple_scab.treatment_note: Apply locally approved protectant or systemic fungicides timed with weather-based disease forecasting models. Alternate FRAC groups to prevent resistance development.

symptoms: Small purple flecks enlarging into circular 'frogeye' spots with tan centers and purple margins.
Firm, dark rotting areas with concentric rings on fruit.
Cankers forming on limbs and branches.
causes: Fungal pathogen Botryosphaeria obtusa.
Pathogen infects through natural openings, wounds, or dead tissue.
environment: Warm, humid conditions (68°F to 80°F / 20°C to 27°C)
Frequent precipitation and canopy shading
spread: Rain splash and air currents dispersing conidia from branch cankers and mummified fruit.
immediate_actions: Prune out dead wood, cankered limbs, and fire blight strikes at least 6-8 inches below visible symptoms.
Collect and destroy mummified fruit clinging to trees or on the ground.
prevention: Maintain tree vigor with balanced nutrition and proper pruning.
Prevent mechanical and insect injury to bark and fruit.
apple_black_rot.treatment_note: Apply approved broad-spectrum fungicides from petal fall through cover sprays in conjunction with rigorous cultural sanitation.

symptoms: Bright yellow-orange circular spots on the upper leaf surface.
Small raised tubelike fungal structures (aecia) protruding from the lower leaf surface.
Yellow spots with raised margins on the calyx end of fruit.
causes: Gymnosporangium juniperi-virginianae (obligate heteroecious fungus requiring both apple and eastern red cedar/juniper hosts).
environment: Wet spring weather (50°F to 75°F / 10°C to 24°C)
Presence of galls on nearby juniper trees during rainy periods
spread: Windborne teliospores from juniper galls travel up to several miles to infect apple foliage.
immediate_actions: Document infection severity across the orchard block.
Identify and eradicate nearby wild eastern red cedar trees within a 1-2 mile radius if feasible.
prevention: Select rust-resistant apple varieties (e.g., Enterprise, Freedom, Priscilla).
Prune cedar galls from ornamental junipers before orange gelatinous horns emerge in spring.
apple_cedar_apple_rust.treatment_note: Apply sterol inhibitor (DMI) or strobilurin (QoI) fungicides starting at tight cluster through petal fall when wet weather coincides with gall sporulation.

symptoms: Oval to elongate cinnamon-brown powdery pustules on both upper and lower leaf surfaces.
Pustules rupture the epidermis releasing rust-colored urediniospores.
Severe infections lead to chlorosis, necrosis, and premature leaf drying.
causes: Fungal pathogen Puccinia sorghi.
environment: Moderate temperatures (60°F to 77°F / 16°C to 25°C)
High relative humidity (>95%) and extended dew periods
spread: Spores carried long distances on southerly wind currents from subtropical regions.
immediate_actions: Scout upper canopy leaves (especially ear leaf and adjacent leaves) during early reproductive stages.
Determine threshold: fungicide application may be warranted if pustules cover >5-10% of ear leaf area before blister/milk stage.
prevention: Plant corn hybrids with specific (Rp) or general multi-gene resistance.
Time planting to avoid peak regional spore flights.
corn_common_rust.treatment_note: Apply registered dual-mode fungicides (e.g. triazole + strobilurin) if disease reaches economic threshold on susceptible hybrids before grain fill.

symptoms: Small, tan spots with yellow halos expanding into long, narrow, rectangular gray-to-tan lesions.
Lesion margins strictly bordered by leaf veins.
Extensive blighting of upper canopy during grain fill.
causes: Fungal pathogen Cercospora zeae-maydis.
Survives in corn crop residue on the soil surface.
environment: Warm temperatures (75°F to 86°F / 24°C to 30°C)
High humidity and prolonged dew (>12 hours)
spread: Wind and splashing rain transport conidia from residue to lower leaves, progressing upward.
immediate_actions: Scout lower leaves before tassel (VT) stage; monitor progression toward the ear leaf.
Assess hybrid susceptibility rating.
prevention: Select high-tolerance corn hybrids.
Rotate crops with non-host species (e.g. soybean) for at least one year.
Manage crop residue in high-risk continuous corn fields.
corn_gray_leaf_spot.treatment_note: Apply labeled foliar fungicides between VT and R2 stages if disease is present on third leaf below ear leaf or higher on susceptible hybrids.

symptoms: Large, long, elliptical/cigar-shaped grayish-green to tan lesions (1 to 6 inches long).
Dark fungal sporulation visible within lesions under humid conditions.
causes: Fungal pathogen Exserohilum turcicum (Setosphaeria turcica).
environment: Moderate temperatures (65°F to 80°F / 18°C to 27°C)
Frequent rain, heavy dews, and persistent leaf wetness
spread: Conidia dislodged from residue by rain and wind.
immediate_actions: Scout field from mid-whorl to silking stage.
Evaluate disease pressure on ear leaf and leaves above ear.
prevention: Plant hybrids carrying Ht resistance genes.
Implement crop rotation and residue management practices.
corn_northern_leaf_blight.treatment_note: Treat with approved triazole or strobilurin fungicides when threshold is reached prior to soft dough stage on high-yield potential crops.

symptoms: Small, circular reddish-brown spots on leaves surrounded by dark brown margins and tiny black pycnidia.
Fruit berries turn soft, brown, and then shrivel into hard, black, wrinkled mummies.
causes: Fungal pathogen Guignardia bidwellii (Phyllosticta ampelicida).
environment: Warm, wet weather (70°F to 85°F / 21°C to 29°C)
Rainfall and extended canopy wetness (6 to 24 hours)
spread: Ascospores and conidia dispersed by rain splash from overwintered mummies and cane lesions.
immediate_actions: Remove and destroy mummified grape clusters from vines and ground.
Prune infected canes during dormant season.
prevention: Canopy management (hedging, leaf pulling) to enhance rapid drying.
Apply protective fungicides from early shoot growth through 4-5 weeks post-bloom.
grape_black_rot.treatment_note: Protect flower clusters and young fruit from early bloom through verasion using labeled DMI, QoI, or protectant fungicides (mancozeb, captan).

symptoms: 'Tiger-stripe' leaf pattern: chlorotic and necrotic areas between main leaf veins.
Small dark spots ('measles') on white and red grape berries.
Spongy white heartwood rot in mature trunks.
causes: Complex of vascular fungi including Phaeomoniella chlamydospora, Phaeoacremonium minimum, and Fomitiporia mediterranea.
environment: Hot summer temperatures triggering sudden apoplexy or chronic foliar decline.
Infection occurs through large pruning wounds during wet winter periods.
spread: Airborne and waterborne spores entering open pruning wounds on perennial wood.
immediate_actions: Mark symptomatic vines in summer for targeted dormant remediation.
Prune dead cordons back to clean, white, symptom-free wood.
prevention: Delay winter pruning until late dormant season (sap flow helps push out spores).
Treat all large pruning wounds with pruning sealant or biocontrol (Trichoderma) paste.
grape_esca.treatment_note: No curative chemical cure exists for internal trunk decay; preventive wound protection and trunk renewal/grafting are standard management practices.

symptoms: Irregular brown to dark reddish-brown foliar spots with distinct margins.
Lesions may coalesce causing broad marginal leaf necrosis and defoliation.
causes: Pseudocercospora vitis (Isariopsis clavispora).
environment: Warm, humid conditions late in the growing season.
Overcrowded vine canopies with poor ventilation.
spread: Wind and splash-dispersed fungal conidia.
immediate_actions: Facilitate canopy airflow by selective leaf removal around fruiting zones.
prevention: Standard post-harvest vineyard sanitation.
Maintain fungicide spray programs through late summer in high-humidity regions.
grape_leaf_blight.treatment_note: Apply registered copper or broad-spectrum vineyard fungicides according to regional extension calendars.

symptoms: Small dark brown to black spots on older leaves.
Lesions enlarge with characteristic 'target-board' concentric rings.
Affected leaves yellow, dry up, and drop prematurely.
causes: Fungal pathogen Alternaria solani.
Favored by crop stress, low soil fertility, and frequent wetting cycles.
environment: Warm temperatures (75°F to 85°F / 24°C to 29°C)
Alternating wet and dry periods (dew/overhead irrigation followed by warm sunshine)
spread: Windblown and splash-dispersed conidia from infected crop debris and solanaceous weeds.
immediate_actions: Inspect lower canopy foliage.
Avoid excess overhead irrigation late in the afternoon to minimize nighttime leaf wetness.
prevention: Implement 3-year crop rotation away from solanaceous crops.
Maintain adequate plant nitrogen and potassium nutrition.
Destroy volunteer potato plants and nightshade weeds.
potato_early_blight.treatment_note: Apply protectant fungicides (chlorothalonil, mancozeb) starting before canopy closure, alternating with FRAC 7, 9, or 11 products.

symptoms: Large, irregular water-soaked pale-to-dark green lesions that turn purplish-brown to black.
Delicate white fungal-like growth visible on leaf undersides during moist mornings.
Tuber decay with brown, granular dry rot beneath the skin.
causes: Oomycete pathogen Phytophthora infestans (highly aggressive water mold).
environment: Cool, damp weather (60°F to 70°F / 15°C to 21°C)
Relative humidity >90% and continuous leaf wetness
spread: Airborne sporangia can travel tens of miles on cloudy, humid days; zoospores swim in free water films.
immediate_actions: URGENT: Isolate affected field sections immediately to prevent catastrophic epidemic spread.
Destroy and bag heavily infected plants without shaking spores onto healthy rows.
Notify regional agricultural extension alert services.
prevention: Plant only certified disease-free seed tubers.
Eliminate cull piles and volunteer potatoes before planting season.
Monitor blight forecasting systems (e.g. Blitecast).
potato_late_blight.treatment_note: Apply targeted oomycete fungicides (mandipropamid, cyazofamid, fluopicolide) on strict 5-7 day intervals during high-risk weather. Use preventive protectants prior to infection.

symptoms: Dark brown to black lesions with concentric rings ('target' pattern) on lower foliage.
Yellow halos surrounding maturing spots.
Stem cankers and dark, sunken leathery rot at the stem end of fruit.
causes: Fungal pathogen Alternaria solani / Alternaria linariae.
environment: Warm, humid conditions (75°F to 85°F / 24°C to 30°C)
Frequent overhead watering, rain, and heavy dew
spread: Conidia transported by wind, rain splash, tools, and workers.
immediate_actions: Prune off lower infected leaves touching the soil surface.
Stake and cage plants to keep foliage elevated off wet ground.
prevention: Apply organic or plastic mulch beneath plants to create a barrier against soilborne spores.
Use drip irrigation rather than overhead sprinklers.
Rotate out of solanaceous crops for 2-3 years.
tomato_early_blight.treatment_note: Use registered copper, chlorothalonil, or bio-fungicides on a preventative schedule starting at first sign of lower foliar spotting.

symptoms: Rapidly expanding water-soaked greasy gray-green lesions on leaves and stems.
White fuzzy sporulation on the underside of leaves in high humidity.
Firm, greasy, golden-brown to dark lesions on green and ripening fruit.
causes: Oomycete pathogen Phytophthora infestans.
environment: Cool, rainy, overcast weather (60°F to 75°F / 15°C to 24°C)
Prolonged humidity >90%
spread: Microscopic sporangia carried on wind currents and splashing water.
immediate_actions: Remove and bag infected plants during dry midday conditions to prevent spore dispersion.
Do not compost infected tissue; discard or bury deeply.
prevention: Choose late-blight resistant tomato varieties (e.g., Defiant, Mountain Merit, Jasper, Plum Regal).
Ensure maximum plant spacing and full sun exposure.
Avoid working in tomato beds when leaves are wet.
tomato_late_blight.treatment_note: Apply oomycete-targeted preventative treatments (copper, phosphonates, or specialized translaminar fungicides) ahead of forecast rain periods.

symptoms: Small (1/8 inch), dark brown to black circular lesions with water-soaked margins.
Severe leaf blighting, yellowing, and defoliation.
Small, dark, raised blister-like spots on green fruit which later become scab-like.
causes: Bacterial complex Xanthomonas perforans, X. euvesicatoria, X. gardneri, and X. vesicatoria.
environment: Warm temperatures (75°F to 86°F / 24°C to 30°C)
High rainfall, driving storms, and overhead irrigation
spread: Bacteria enter through natural openings (stomata, hydathodes) and micro-wounds created by windblown sand or equipment.
immediate_actions: Sanitize pruning shears between plants with 70% alcohol or 10% bleach solution.
Avoid handling or harvesting wet foliage.
prevention: Use certified disease-free, hot-water-treated seeds and transplants.
Employ drip irrigation to eliminate splash dispersal.
tomato_bacterial_spot.treatment_note: Apply preventative fixed copper bactericides combined with mancozeb or plant defense inducers (Acibenzolar-S-methyl / Actigard) where copper resistance occurs.

symptoms: Severe stunting and erect 'bushy' growth habit of plants.
Upward cupping and yellowing (chlorosis) of leaf margins.
Significant reduction in leaf size and severe blossom drop leading to minimal fruit set.
causes: Begomovirus (TYLCV) transmitted by the sweetpotato / silverleaf whitefly (Bemisia tabaci).
environment: Warm to hot climates supporting high whitefly vector populations.
Greenhouse and field tomato production zones.
spread: Persistent transmission by adult whiteflies feeding on phloem sap.
immediate_actions: Rogue out and destroy infected plants showing virus symptoms immediately to reduce viral reservoir.
Deploy yellow sticky traps to monitor whitefly vector density.
prevention: Plant TYLCV-resistant hybrids carrying Ty-1, Ty-2, or Ty-3 resistance genes.
Use fine mesh insect netting (50 mesh) in greenhouse/nursery production.
Apply reflective silver mulches to repel whitefly landings.
tomato_yellow_leaf_curl_virus.treatment_note: No chemical viricide can cure systemic viral infections. Control whitefly vectors using integrated pest management (soaps, oils, and rotating insecticides).

symptoms: Small circular purple-to-reddish spots on upper leaf surfaces.
Centers of lesions turn brown, die, and may drop out leaving a 'shot-hole' appearance.
Leaves turn bright yellow and drop prematurely, often defoliating trees by mid-summer.
causes: Fungal pathogen Blumeriella jaapii (Higginsia jaapii).
environment: Moderate temperatures (60°F to 68°F / 15°C to 20°C)
Frequent spring rains and extended canopy wetness (>5 hours)
spread: Ascospores discharged from overwintered leaves on the orchard floor during spring rain events.
immediate_actions: Collect and mulch or remove fallen infected leaves beneath trees.
Prune to open tree canopy and promote rapid foliar drying.
prevention: Apply protective fungicides starting at petal fall and continuing at 10-14 day intervals through post-harvest.
Mow or apply nitrogen fertilizer to orchard floor in autumn to speed leaf degradation.
cherry_leaf_spot.treatment_note: Use captan, chlorothalonil, or sterol inhibitors (myclobutanil, fenbuconazole) according to fruit tree extension guidelines.

symptoms: Small, yellowish-green spots with water-soaked borders on leaves.
Lesions turn brown, become necrotic, and cause severe lower leaf drop.
Rough, raised, warty brown lesions on pepper fruits.
causes: Xanthomonas euvesicatoria and Xanthomonas vesicatoria.
environment: High temperatures (75°F to 90°F / 24°C to 32°C)
High relative humidity, wind-driven rains, and sprinkler irrigation
spread: Splashing water, contaminated seed, workers, and field equipment.
immediate_actions: Cease overhead irrigation immediately; switch to ground-level drip.
Do not enter fields while foliage is damp.
prevention: Plant pepper varieties bred for bacterial spot resistance (e.g. races 1-10).
Treat seeds with hot water (122°F / 50°C for 25 minutes) before sowing.
Maintain a 2-year non-host rotation.
pepper_bacterial_spot.treatment_note: Apply preventative copper sprays mixed with mancozeb, or use systemic acquired resistance boosters (Actigard) before infection occurs.

symptoms: White, talcum-powder-like circular fungal spots on upper and lower leaf surfaces, petioles, and stems.
Infected leaves turn yellow, brown, and become brittle, exposing fruit to sunscald.
causes: Podosphaera xanthii (syn. Sphaerotheca fuliginea) and Golovinomyces cichoracearum.
environment: Warm, dry days with high relative humidity at night (68°F to 80°F / 20°C to 27°C)
Dense, shaded plant canopies (does not require free water on leaves to infect)
spread: Abundant windblown conidia capable of traveling long distances.
immediate_actions: Inspect lower and crown leaves where shaded microclimates favor early development.
Remove severely infested older leaves if canopy density allows.
prevention: Select powdery-mildew resistant squash and pumpkin cultivars.
Space plants generously to optimize sunlight exposure and air movement.
squash_powdery_mildew.treatment_note: Apply sulfur, potassium bicarbonate, neem oil, or registered DMI/QoI fungicides upon first detection of powdery colonies on lower leaves.

symptoms: Numerous small, irregular purplish spots on upper leaf surfaces.
Lesions coalesce, causing leaf margins to curl upward and look burnt or 'scorched'.
Dark lesions on petioles, fruit pedicels, and sepals (caps).
causes: Fungal pathogen Diplocarpon earlianum.
environment: Moderate to warm temperatures (60°F to 75°F / 15°C to 24°C)
Frequent rain, overhead irrigation, and prolonged leaf wetness
spread: Conidia dislodged and splashed by water droplets from overwintered leaves.
immediate_actions: Renovate strawberry beds after harvest: mow, discard, or incorporate old foliage.
Avoid night watering.
prevention: Plant certified disease-free strawberry crowns.
Maintain narrow row widths and weed control for quick canopy drying.
Select less susceptible cultivars (e.g. Allstar, Honeoye).
strawberry_leaf_scorch.treatment_note: Apply protectant fungicides (captan, thiram) or systemic fungicides in spring when new growth starts and during wet weather cycles.
